OK, so I downloaded and tried to install this program on my Windows 7 64-bit OS.  The program H&R Block Premium Home and Business has two components, H&R Block 2011 (this is your personal tax software), the second is the H&R Block Business 2011 (this is your business tax software, i.e. LLC, Corp, etc). I found no problems with H&R Block 2011, but had major problems with H&R Block Business 2011.  Installation errors indicated that OLE2.DLL is not compatible...  When I tried to start H&R Block Business 2011, I could not update or move through the program without it crashing.  After several hours of effort, I finally found a solution. First off, I have to say that H&R Block is EXTREMELY LAZY in how they process installation files. Essentially, I discovered that they placed numerous files (called .ocx files) in the wrong locations, a major flaw in their approach.  First off, go to the directory where the program was installed. Since I am using Windows 7 64-bit, my program was installed in the following directory:  c:\program files(x86)\H&R Block Business 2011\  Note: If you are using a 32-bit version of Windows, it will most likely be under c:\program files\H&R Block Business 2011\  Once you have navigated to the appropriate folder, look for a file called \\"!Tax2011_Errors.log\\"  Open the file with Notepad.exe  This file is critical because it lists all of the problems that H&R Block Business is having during its use.  Mine indicated that files RICHTX32.OCX and MSCOMCTL.OCX were not properly registered. What that means is that the program cannot find them or they do not exist.  I found these programs in C:\Windows\system32 folder. However, this is the wrong location for Windows 7 64-bit. This is not a 64-bit program, H&R Block software is 32-bit, which is completely distinct. These files must be located in the C:\Windows\sysWOW64\ folder.  Simply copy the files from the C:\windows\system32 to the C:\Windows\sysWOW64 folder.  After you have copied the software to the correct folder, you may also need to register or activate these files as well. To do that, you need to open a command prompt (click Start, type cmd in the search field and choose cmd.exe)  at the c:\ type the following  regsvr32.exe c:\windows\sysWOW64\richtx32.ocx  then press enter and wait a couple of seconds and you should see a dialog box that says it was successful  back at the c:\ prompt type the following  regsvr32.exe c:\windows\sysWOW64\mscomctl.ocx  then press enter and wait a couple of seconds and you should see a dialog box that says it was successfull  You should now be able to use H&R Block Business 2011. Remember that the log file will help to identify your problem, and if it is not the one described above, you should be able to dissect the problem.  Good Luck,  James

I was a PC user recently converted to Mac in April 2013. With that said, I have had a lot of adjustments to get used to in general as a Mac does not work the same a PC does. My banking transition was the most aggravating issue for me after testing out Quicken 2007 for Mac and Quicken Essentials for Mac and realizing that they were nothing like the Quicken 2006 for PC that I had been using. We even considered running parallels just to use my old version of Quicken on the Mac but I had lost my Quicken product Key information so this was not an option.
I had been a loyal Quicken user since 2003. I also had been a loyal Quickbooks for PC user to create invoices and printing checks, to use for our personal business. With that said, I will give my overall opinion of how I think iBank4 stacks against Intuit (Quicken & Quickbooks) products.

Pros:
-There are helpful online video tutorials.
-There is a live chat forum offered for iBank through business hours in the week. (I would rate them 5 stars if it was just based on their helpful and quick chat responses). Quicken fails in this area.
-I can adjust font settings in the check printing set up (love this!) as well as reposition the fields so that they line up perfectly on my check vouchers when printed.
-I can designate color in the categories window for different categories like household purchases, dining, or automotive. Very helpful and makes for a distinct check register when I look at it!!! So brilliant!
-I can add little icons pictures to my categories as well (like a soccer ball which represents my recreation category, or a french fries icon photo which represents dining out category). This is my most favorite feature coupled with the colored categories. I love it!!!
-I can pull any type of report and be as specific or non specific as I want, stretching the time amount for the report from a day to ten years or more if I choose.
-I was able to bring over the last 10 years worth of banking that was stored in Quicken.
-I was able to successfully bring over my Quickbooks bank register information into iBank4 (this requires some reading from the IGG knowledge base answer from John who describes how to do this by exporting with a CSV file format)

Cons:
- Many function keys at the bottom are masked with symbols (+ or - key, register key symbol and reconcile key symbol). This was a turn off because I did not automatically understand what each key represented and I had to learn these key functions
-I must add a new transaction with the plus (+) key in bank4. (With Intuit's products, the enter key begins a new transaction.)
-The only way I can toggle between the different sections (date, category, payee field, amount etc) of a transaction entry in iBank4 is with the tab key. Intuit products allowed the enter key to toggle between the date, category, payee field, amount etc, as well as allowing me to move through each entry in the check register by pressing enter. In iBank4, the enter key is more like a save function and to move between transactions the mouse must be used.
- When pressing the plus (+) key for a new transaction entry, a blank entry is allowed. This to me is my biggest CON with iBank software. Why is a blank entry even allowed? I did not have this problem with either Quicken or Quickbooks.
- Moving information over from Quicken and Quickbooks and setting up a catch all Reconcile statement within iBank4 is a little tedious since reconcile statements do not move over in the transfer to iBank.
- I had to discover (the hard way) that I needed to set the Opening Balance in the reconcile setup of each of my IBank accounts to a zero balance since my original opening balance in Quicken/Quickbooks was shown as a check register deposit entry. Heads up to users like me who confuse this action and enter the opening balance amount not knowing it must be set to zero *if* a deposit is shown inthe register as your original opening balance. Maybe they add this action for some banks who do not show opening deposits as a deposit when you open an account, if that's the case, I understand why it is given. But I do feel they could offer a better explanation so that users do not trip up on this part in the whole initial set up process and thus making their impression of iBank a good one.
- A report in iBank4 cannot be created by the right click key function that I could do in Quicken. But you can create virtually any report you need with their add report button (+ button key in bottom left hand corner) and just specify the functions you need it to run.

I am a little over six weeks into my total use of iBank4. My opinion of their software is intended to help you better decide if iBank is for you if you are considering a move from Quicken to a better alternative on a Mac. I do feel iBank4 is the best banking software available on a Mac and I do believe that they will improve as they grow as a company.I would encourage you to test out iBank's 30 day free trial version and ask your questions to them during that time to see if it's the right choice for you. It was the right choice for me and I am happy with their software. :)

I've been a loyal TT customer for 10+ years like many of you. And, duly insulted by Intuit's money grab, I decided to go with H&R Block. So if you were wondering which worked best...read on.

In a nutshell I got a $600 higher Federal refund and a state tax penalty that was $155 less by using TurboTax.

There are several reasons why. TurboTax does a more thorough job importing prior year's data and matching it side-by-side, making it much easier to note changes. H&R only imported my demographics. The interview process is more polished in TT, and thoroughly fleshed out my tax situation, which made it more straightforward to discover valid deductions. Here's two important examples where H&R faltered: I have an adult child who I can claim as a qualified relative, but the interview process totally dropped the ball. I had to drill into the forms to manually capture them as a dependent, an important deduction. Later I entered student loan interest from two lenders, but when I reviewed the final return only one of them had an entry. I again drilled down into the forms to find that a check box had been omitted on a lender, leading H&R to believe the interest wasn't tax deductible. A potential $2000 difference. And there was nothing in the interview process to have led me to make that choice in error.

So even after correcting the flaws and running both programs all the way though, TurboTax still managed a more favorable result.

H&R Block is cheaper - no two ways about it. And it works quite well. But I believe you have to be more astute to avoid unexpected results. And for those who are truly paranoid about an audit here is the difference between the programs. H&R will provide someone to attend an audit with you for free. TurboTax has a $60 fee, but the (optional) service from TaxAudit means they will fully review your return and do battle before the IRS. You have no involvement. Pick your poison.

So there's my experience. What I got back by using TurboTax more than made up for the higher expense (and this year's profound aggravation).

Almost none of the other reviews are rating the actual product. Keep in mind that I recognize that MS has drastically changed the price of Office and I don't like it any more than you. But I feel it is still important to review the product so that you can judge for yourself if the product warrants its price. If you can't find Office 2010 Home and Student (3 PC's) or need more than Excel, PowerPoint, or Word then here are the 2013 MSRP prices:

Home and Student $140 - 1PC
Home and Business $220 - 1PC
Office Professional $400 - 1PC
Office 365 Home Premium $99/Year - 5 licenses for any device (PC, Mac, supported tablet). Licenses can be switched to another device at any time.
Office 365 Small Business Premium - $150.00 user/year or $15.00 user/month. 1-10 employees Each user gets to put office on 5 devices(PC, supported tablets, *Mac but I'm not positive*)

Unless you buy Office 365, you are stuck with this one license for your one computer.Also keep in mind that Office 2013 is only for Windows 7, 8.
Obviously if you have more than 1 computer, then Office 365 may be the way to go (for home use). Businesses will have to judge for themselves, but now that you can transfer licenses to other computers, the standalone may be the better choice. Yes, it's subscription based, but every 3 or 4 years when the next version of Office is released it will have been cheaper than buying 5 individual licenses. I say that based on current pricing models. The 365 model has any future upgrades included. If you only have 1 PC then any of the versions will do you fine.

Now onto the product itself, sort of.. I have used all products in the new Office suite including Visio and Project but I have not used OneNote. This version of Office is truly the best yet. Everything can be tied into Skydrive (cloud storage) so your files can follow you. This may not be new for the industry but is new for Office. When you hit 'Save As' it will ask for a location and one of the choices is your Skydrive account. I notice a significant speed boost when any of the programs load up compared to 2010 versions. The new office is fast, as it should be. The ribbon is very familiar and the whole UI is straight forward. You won't find any curves or color in the new Office however. The look has been simplified but many will feel it isn't as visually appealing as previous versions. With that said, I do like the look. Let's be honest here though, no one has ever bought Office because it looks pretty. With that said there's nothing crazy revolutionary about it, but a nice step forward. Visio still has default bland general objects that look nothing like what your trying to visualize. Excel, Word and all the rest work great.

A key point is that you can edit and save PDF's in Word now. However, the more graphics in the PDF, the more Word screws up. The commenting and review feature has been given a major upgrade. It now has tree-structured comment boxes that you can minimize and mark as \\"done\\". The spell check dialog is now in a panel to the right of the editing window. This makes the spell check process far less annoying.
In excel, if you highlight a block of data the little lightning bolt box appears but now has many useful formatting options. It is a better alternative than hunting through the ribbon. Something called \\"Flash Fill\\" fills in a new column of data with data taken from other columns without making you scratch your head about a formula. Do a google search to see what i mean. Graphs and charts change as soon as you change a number in a table. So you can quickly see the result without having to remake the graph.

This may have been a feature in Outlook 2010 but you can now hide the ribbon and you can use a smaller toolbar instead. The File, Home, Send etc stay visible. You can choose from only a couple of themes for you background to help with the dull, bland feel. Searching has been improved to allow searching through not only mail but subject, attachments, and calender. Outlook 2013 has integrated with some social media like linkedIn. Your contacts can show up, along with updates and what not. If you have Microsoft Lync, you can schedule appointments to meet in person or on Lync. Tasks can be synced through outlook.com If Outlook is you work life then that should help simplify appointments and regular tasks to be checked off all on one calender available on the web (outlook.com).

Security software is well-known for causing systems to run poorly, tying up valuable resources, causing long startup and/or shutdown times, or running at the worst possible, most inconvenient times.

This software changes all of that... sets the bar VERY high for the other software in the same class.

Under normal conditions, this software uses a whopping 20mb of my ram. To put it into perspective, my firefox browser uses 185mb and Internet Explorer uses 125mb. Now granted, I have 16gb of ram, which, admittedly, is overkill, so even if I had 2 or 4 gigs, this software would still run very lightly.

I have bounced back and forth between apple products and windows products (I'm NOT a Microsoft fan), and I've never used anti-virus software on any of my macs and never had any issues, but I wouldn't dare do that on my Windows PC. I often forget that I even have anti-virus software.

I ascribe my problems to inadequate software testing before product marketing. Simply that.

That said, Quicken is basically a flat database that can be sorted/grouped/classified and queried. Queries are presented as dialog boxes (Windows lingo) that allow for Boolean logic in a friendly way. Not much different from previous versions.
This version combines the QEL, IDX, etc files into a single QDF data file. Convenient for what it's worth. Here'smy personal beef with a much touted feature.
A bank reconciliation is an internal check on one's own book-keeping but, more so,a check on the bank to ensure there are no errors, nobody else is dipping into your pocket, etc. Why, on earth, should one download transactions off the bank's books and adopt same as a personal archive to rely on. Makes sense to download investment ddata, W-2s for tax prep, etc. but not for day-to-day banking. This last comment is humbly presented, based on a mere forty years of public, professional accounting and auditing and several years of University. Feel free to disagree.

After many happy years with Money (stuck at 2003), being able to manage my financials in a superlative and reliable fashion, the removal of support for is its simple institutional integration forced me to bite the bullet and move to... well, all there is now is Mint and Quicken (now a unified Monopoly, the same one that killed the simple earlier integration with promises of improvement).

It is quite possible that at one point Quicken was as good, but the current product is a nightmare of epic proportions. It would appear that after obviously cornering the market, Intuit has done nothing to leverage that into a superior product, instead it degrades with nothing of value left to compare it to. Here is a case where the free market has failed.

May I remind everyone, it is pretty simple: a date, a description, a credit or debit amount. And yet, this basic idea is lost in a maze of complexity inundated with failures.

While I find he interface poorly designed, a legacy set of junk that appears to have grow over the years such that the basics have fallen through the cracks, I need not waste my time on looking there. Why? Because I can't get my data in, nor trust what is there will be useful in the future.

To start, bringing in any of the history we all have requires one to jump though creative nightmarish hoops, for which the result is crap shoot (in the end I made a new \\"cash account\\" and imported one account at a time there and \\"cut 'n paste\\" into other accounts). Should one get in (either via luck with importing games or by throwing in the towel and abandoning your history), anything goes wrong and you are at the mercy of losing everything due to the complexity. Here, after 30 years of programming, I am entitle to jump to conclusions here about the cause: legacy complexity of too many esoteric features overwhelming the basics.

The most important point of a product like this is to gather this simple information from all the varied account interfaces (checking, savings, credit cards, brokerage, retirement) into one central interface. Yet institutional integration is hit or miss, with neither institutions nor Intuit caring.

Face it: no one is going to type in all their transactions. So, you darn well better be sure your institution works with Quicken or it will be useless. And, when it breaks, do not expect a fix - you are back to manual. This is the Achilles heel: you can't trust it with your history because you don't know what will happen tomorrow.

My conclusions are based on my own experience. My Bank Account would not download until after about 20 useless emails with support over 1 month, where they barely read anything I wrote. In the end I found the problem with Quicken (could not handle two accounts on one institution with the same \\"account name\\") by learning about and deciphering the Quicken logs I had sent them. After this they did not care about knowing this shortcoming. And the, one of my three credit cards that was supported was sold to another company without my consent... not supported any longer, and so now what do I do with that history and future? Finally, my major 401k at ADP (not a small company, I am sure you have heard of them) is not supported. Do they care? Will it be? Nope.

My conclusions are further supported by searching and finding that this is the same for zillions. How can it be that a company with a Monopoly in this market space gets mediocre and less reviews from most users? It is embarrassing.

There are many of you that use Quicken and have settled into a routine since you were lucky enough to find \\"things that worked\\". More power to you. But it is just a matter time before it goes bad for you. Probably the next \\"forced\\" upgrade, and/or when your financial institution is sold to another in this current way Wall St works.

As for new users considering this product: good luck, maybe you to will get\\"in\\". But, again, your future is dismal.

And for all of us, there is no hope in view. We are worse off than a decade ago, and with each release Quicken deteriorates as shown by intelligent reviews of those who have been with it for years. Alternatively Mint is barely holding on, for those willing to trust all their data to the \\"Mint\\" server which could go offline any time just like Intuit's previous online money site \\"Quicken Online\\".

What am I doing? Well, struggling with Quicken and Mint in parallel daily, hoping to \\"survive\\". What a wonderful set of products.

I was able to create a very serviceable website using a provided template and had it published in about 30 minutes. The design elements are easy to edit and adjust, and the drag and drop features make it easy for the low level designer to get a good looking website built for themselves.

There are a lot of positives I could write about, but rather than a 1,000 word review, I'll just say this is a great tool for novice webmasters. I used to use Dreamweaver but that is a lot more advanced and requires a good deal of knowledge so it's not recommended for beginners.

On the downside, there's not enough ability to edit the raw HTML. There are times when that would be helpful. Perhaps in a newer release they could consider allowing the user to get at the raw HTML engine. But so far it has not limited me from accomplishing what I've wanted to do. You can add HTML code to the body and head, but you're not privy to the full code; it simply adds it in a properties box. Again, it works, but most of us web designers want that raw editing ability. I assume Xara did this to limit the damage a novice could do with a few errant commands or keystrokes. And, working outside of the provided templates is a bit less intuitive, and in my opinion there just aren't enough unique templates available to work with.

These are quite desirable today; in short, the website adapts itself to the size of the user's display, which eliminates the need for a second mobile site and subsequent redirection. The greatest limitation of this product is that you are confined to 2 dimensional drawing. If you need 3 dimensional abilities, this LT should be avoided in favour of the main, full Autocad. Having said this, suppose 2D works for you. Perhaps you are working on something whose final output is intrinsically 2D, rather than, say, a 3D set of objects where you will ultimately take a rendering at some angle. Then Autocad LT is a very economical choice, rather than paying for functionality you do not need.

For experienced Autocad users, the ability to customise the work environment is a serious plus. It lets you drag along from your use of earlier Autocad versions the personal optimisation you've engendered. You won't feel like you are starting afresh in a new Autocad. This compatibility is extended to the data you or others have already made in PDF and DWG formats, along with other industry standards like JPEG and Tif. The documentation also refers to reading Microsoft Excel files. I did not have occasion to use these, but perhaps it's useful to you.

Autosnapping is quite useful. Especially where you can avail yourself of drawing a geometrically regular object. Purists who are artists who need a full freehand ability and associated tools like brushes should look to other packages. LT is meant more for a mechanical design or architectural blueprints.

If you are new to Autocad, try getting this accompanying book for a comprehensive support, AutoCAD 2013 and AutoCAD LT 2013 Essentials. It is specific to this LT 2013 version, and may save you much time in climbing the learning curve.

This review concerns only the download and installation experience for this product, Rosetta Stone Dutch, level 1, for Mac. As I use the product I might update this review.  As a Mac user, I'm accustomed to buying software on the App Store. Download and installation is automatic and fast. The download/install process for this product is as far from that experience as one could imagine. It's stunningly terrible, and I am not being hyperbolic.  First you need to download, mount, and launch Amazon's proprietary download software. What? In 2015?  Then, using Amazon's software, you download the product, which arrives in a disk image. You run the installer from the disk image, supplying your admin credentials.  Then you launch the software you bought, and rather than starting to use it, you are required to start updating. For me, I had to go through a sequence of two updates, each of which required download (each well over 100 MB), admin password entry, and acceptance of terms and conditions.  So, about 45 minutes in to this process (that's if you're lucky enough to have very fast broadband to accommodate the four downloads you've performed), you again try launching the product you bought. This time it does not prompt for yet another update. Yay? No. It asks you to insert your CD-ROM disk.  Of course, as a download product, there is no CD-ROM disk.  After trying various approaches to get around this problem, which included searching first on Amazon for help and then on the Rosetta Stone support pages for help, I was, one could say, well surprised but not delighted.  I then found, buried deep behind a labyrinth of unhelpful content on the Rosetta Stone site, a link to initiate a live chat session. Which I did. If the single star I've awarded indicates anything positive, it's that they do offer chat support, and it's available apparently any time of day.  The person who helped me was indeed able to help me solve the problem, but only because I could second guess his poor instructions. For example, he wrote "click" the the chat window when he meant "double click," and he asked me to move a file from a mounted disk image to the Desktop when that step is entirely unnecessary. In our chat, he wrote wonderfully ambiguous instructions such as "Please drag the file."  It turned out that to use the software I purchased, I had to use Finder to navigate to a hidden folder, create a new folder within it, name that folder with a particular case-sensitive name, and then drag a 400 MB file from the mounted, original disk image, into the folder I had manually created and named.  Then I could use the software.  Then I had to get past the mandatory registration process (of course, at this point I invented a name, email address, age, and so on, because the company had long since burned any remnant of trustworthiness). But I still couldn't use the program I'd purchased.  The running app then opened my web browser and sent me to an associated website, which prompted me, rather rudely, to install Adobe Flash. No. I just closed that Safari window, and then, back in the app, deselected the checkbox that had been selected by default to always send me to the web.  I wanted to learn a bit of Dutch. Instead I learned that this product, which is just level one of a multilevel sequence and which nominally costs more than a hundred dollars, has a 1995 style installation experience, and a horrible one even given that framing.  Wow.

For those of you who need schedule D within the Deluxe version, I just went through the free upgrade process to Premier to acquire it. Here are my notes (I’m using a Macbook):

- Purchase Turbotax Deluxe and install
- Perform the process that creates a myturbotax account at Intuit. Be sure to include your address info (at first I didn’t, but they asked me to complete while I was on the phone)
- Within Turbotax, click “Topic List” and navigate to “Stock, Mutual Fund, and Other Investment Sales”
- You should be on a screen that says “Did You Sell Any Investments in 2014?”. Click “Yes”.
- It then should say something like “You need the Premier” version.
- Either on this screen or the next, it will list steps to buy. Step #2 shows a six digit number (like 9-9-9999). Below that is a box to enter a confirmation number.
- NOW call Turbotax (800.445.1875, M-F, 8am-8pm EST)
- After explaining that you have the Deluxe version and you need schedule D, they will ask for the six digit number (including the dashes! Strange.)
- They will provide a pretty long confirmation number that you plug in, dashes and all.
- Click “Continue” and it will say you’re now using the Premier version

I hope this helps someone else. It took me four phone calls, as follows:

1) Before I purchased I called to verify the process. I was told “purchase Deluxe then call back and we’ll upgrade you”
2) After buying and installing, I called again. How do I upgrade, I say. They said “When you’re filling out your taxes and when you’re on schedule D call us and we’ll upgrade you”.
3) Went directly to schedule D (the form. Mistake. I should have been using the interview process). Called back. Talked to a woman. Was placed on hold. Then connection dropped.
4) On same schedule D form. A different woman now is asking me questions that aren’t related to where I am within Turbotax. I thought it’d be as simple as “go to file/enter code…” or something, but it’s not. After about 25 minutes of her poking around and asking others in her office, I finally got the idea that I should work through the interview process and let it decide that I needed the Premier version. Hence the steps above. Total time of this call: 30 mins, 43 sec.

So, one star because Intuit removed schedule D from the Deluxe version. No stars for upgrading me to the Premier version for free, as this is simply a pacification effort to quell the proletariat masses (I know, too much Jack London).

It is the single best option for capturing video from the major services but still has some big flaws. Must annoying is that when beginning to record a Netflix stream and you have it set to the far more convenient 'auto' setting, it thinks that you are recording a new program each time Netflix changes the resolution as it rests bandwidth and buffers. For instance, if I begin recording Pretty In Pink, Netflix starts it out at 640x360, then as it spools up to 854x480 and then to 1280x720, Audials will record it as 3 different recordings. If it smells doesn't break it up, you will get dropped frames at each resolution change. There is no adjustment to fix this.

Secondly, although the resolution and quality settings are very customizable, recordings use a lot of CPU resources; I would say that they are abnormally high, even considering the use of the x264 encoder. I could literally find no setting of any good quality that would record 720p without making out my AMD x4 955 or FX-6100. Frames rate issues seem to exist here, as judder is nearly inevitable. The only way I have found to get any kind of consistent results is to set the encoder to use the .wmv high quality settings and set it to match the frame rate of the source (which generally seems to be 25 fps). The resulting files are huge, about 8GB per hour. I just reencode them to .mkv or .mp4 with Handbrake. Gives me better results than if I had just captured in this format in the first place. I wouldn't even consider trying to capture in 1080p unless I was running an i5 2500k, Octo-core AMD or i7.

I wish that Audials had a queue feature like It's competitor, PlayLater. It allows.you to queue up a couple dozen programs and they just get recorded one after the other. The video quality from Audials CAN definitely be better than Play Later, but when you're just trying to get an entire season of My Little Pony, the queue feature is just a much bigger factor.

Home Designer Architectural 2015 is similar to other home designer packages in that there is a simple up front wizard to help design the basic layout of your dream home. The nice thing is you can create a basic plan with the wizard with all your preferred room dimensions and save it. Then you can come back and rearrange the layout as many ways as you want without having to redo the rooms again. you can generate floor plans from those different versions of room arraignments and see which you like better. After that you need to spend some time with the documentation and the tutorials to learn how to alter the floor plan that gets generated. If you do not take the time to learn the software you will be in for an extremely frustrating time using this or any other design software. Jumping back and forth between the layout view and the rendered 3d view is very helpful in seeing how your changes to doors or windows placement for example impacts the rooms and whatever grand plans you have for that room or rooms. I'm am still learning the software and will admit that I have had several frustrating times trying to get some idea or change to happen as I want it. One of the most infuriating issues for me, and this is not limited to Chief Architect software, is the clumsy and way too complicated method of creating a cabinet for built-in appliances. I've recently run into quota issues for gmail. Along with the need to aggressively delete e-mail to get under the quota, I've finally decided to take backing up my e-mail seriously. This is important, because together with photos, a lot of e-mail is actually useful for searching and remembering details that aren't recorded any other way. Even if you've decided to pay for storage on Gmail, for instance, there's always the chance that your account gets hijacked phished or otherwise deleted/hacked, so having a backed up archive locally protects you in that event.    As a well documented cheapskate, I first tried the free solutions. Mozilla Thunderbird, for instance, is well known and popularly acclaimed. But it was too slow and couldn't really manage huge inboxes. I tried various other solutions before giving up and acquiring an Outlook 2013 license through an employee purchase program at Microsoft.    Setting up Outlook is fairly straightforward, and it auto-configures now for Gmail accounts as well as Hotmail and Yahoo mail. For Google Apps for your domain accounts, however, you have to go through custom configuration. There are a few bugs there, but eventually I got it so that everything sync'd.    Performance is decent. It can't match the search index that's built on the browser based version of gmail, but it's acceptably fast and works even when you're offline. The real feature that made me pay for a license, however, is the auto-archive feature. This essentially lets you move old e-mail into an archive which you can then access and search separately. I did an archive and the machine went away for a few minutes and created a 9GB archive of my e-mail all the way back from 2004. It's searchable, opening the folder isn't fast, but it works and I can apply filters to it and search it after creating an index, which takes forever.    The biggest pain point is that I have to force myself to keep Outlook running. (It's not a hog: 200MB of RAM is all it takes --- keeping aChrome window open to Gmail costs quite a bit more!) The sync with a live server is also somewhat slow: I frequently get a ping on my browser window a few minutes before Outlook fetches the mail. What's also interesting is that while it automagically imports your calendar (and it does a great job of that), it doesn't automatically import contacts, and the auto-complete does not auto-populate.    What auto-archive does not do, unfortunately, is to remove archived e-mail from the IMAP server (in this case GMail). This isn't great, but on the other hand, means I can now very aggressively delete e-mail in the future.    There's a market opportunity somewhere for an e-mail app that doubles as a backup for cloud-based storage, but I'm sure people like me are a rarity (most people don't even backup their photos). However, just like Open Office Spreadsheet was never a good substitute for Excel, there's no serious alternative to Outlook if you need the capability of offline e-mail or archives.    Recommended.

I installed Photoshop Elements 10 on my 2.8 GHz i7 iMac, running System 10.6.8. Since many reviewers of the boxed version have thoroughly discussed the features of Photoshop Elements already, I am focusing this review on my experiences with using PSE in conjunction with Apple iPhoto.

Background
*My main camera is a 7-year old \\"prosumer\\" Nikon. Back when my camera was new, digital SLR's were primarily targeted to professionals and compact digital cameras had extremely limited functionality. Even though prosumer cameras aren't a significant presence in today's digital camera market, these cameras still produce better images than most current compacts due to their relatively large image sensors.
*I also have a collection of images that were scanned from 35mm film prints. Many of these pix have faded colors as well as digital artifacts from the scanning process.

My review perspective
*I use iPhoto as my main photo repository and for simple tasks such as cropping, straightening, and basic exposure adjustments. I want to use Photoshop Elements to do things that are beyond iPhoto's capabilities, including correcting lens distortion on wide-angle shots, cleaning up and enhancing scanned photos, and making extensive alterations to images (such as removing an unwanted bystander from an architectural shot or blurring a distracting background).

Installation
*Total installation time was about 25 minutes. Download time, of course, will vary for each user. If you have a slow Internet connection, you should consider buying the boxed version.
*Users of Little Snitch (a network security utility) need to approve connections to Adobe servers at several points during the installation process.

User experience
*Photoshop Elements is a feature-laden and complex application. As a result, it has a steep learning curve, especially for Mac users. Much of the user interface is un-Mac like. It takes some time to become accustomed to how the program functions.
*Fortunately, the Help system is extensive and includes many step-by-step guides.
*Once you become comfortable using the program, it's a powerful tool for editing and manipulating photographs. In many ways, Photoshop has transformed photography. Now, instead of worrying about exposure, composition, and everything else when you're out shooting, all you need to do is get a halfway decent image of your subject. It's now possible to manipulate pretty much every aspect of a picture in post-processing as long as you have an in-focus image and sufficient pixels to work with.
*The program does everything I wanted it to do initially and, even better, has opened up many new ways to be creative with my photos. The extensive collection of effects, filters, advanced exposure controls, and editing tools has reignited my interest in photography.

Bottom line
*Photoshop Elements is an outstanding application for photographers who need more advanced tools than iPhoto provides. The only real downside for Mac users is that Photoshop Elements is time consuming to learn and requires regular use to maintain one's skills. There is no good personal finance package for a Mac.  I've tried iBank 5.5.3, GnuCash for Mac 2.6.6, Moneydance 2015.5, AceMoney 4.36.1, and now Quicken for Mac 2015.  Each is unsatisfactory in its own way.  This review applies to Quicken for Mac 2015 version 2.5.0, with some comments about comparable programs.  The best thing about Quicken for Mac is that export of Quicken Windows data (via a Windows-based add-on exporter) works reasonably well.  Not all data can be imported into the Quicken for Mac 2015, because it simply doesn't support the same feature set, but I'd rate the process as very good on the average.  The import process is almost as fast as Moneydance, much faster than GnuCash, and much, much faster than iBank (which takes many hours to import the same data that other programs import in minutes).  After import, Quicken for Mac balances are mostly accurate, which can't be said for some other programs.  Speaking of keeping account balances correct: The basic function of a personal finance package is to balance your checkbook and other accounts.  How hard could that be?  Well, much got lost in re-designing Quicken Windows into a Quicken for Mac; and "reconcile to online balance" and "reconcile shares" functionality is gone.  Instead, you get to manually enter starting and ending balance (from printed statements?), then reconcile transactions between those two dates -- only cash, not shares -- and that's even for online accounts downloaded by Quicken for Mac.  Unfortunately, that's not a quick way to balance your checkbook.  Why is a sensible reconciliation feature missing on the Mac version, while the Windows version has it?  It's a mystery, along with many other mysteries.  For example, Quicken for Mac can export transactions as .CSV, but then can't import its own exported .CSV file.  Who comes up with design specifications like that?  Another mystery: A brokerage account has a cash balance but, when asked, Quicken for Mac claims that the"Online Balance" is zero in the "Transactions" view -- yet shows it as "Available Cash" under the "Portfolio" view.  That's a bit schizophrenic.  Others have pointed out that Quicken for Mac falls short in many areas (particularly reporting), when compared to the Windows version.  However, the Windows version (running within a virtual PC on the fastest Mac) became excruciatingly slow over the years.  Every transaction edit results in ~5 seconds of internal updates before anything else can be done -- something is badly engineered in the Windows version.  Quicken for Mac (working on the same data) is quite responsive, perhaps thanks to internal improvements.  These are two very, very different programs, even though they both say "Quicken".  In summary, Quicken for Mac 2015 is not terrible, but it isn't very good either.  It works in a limited way, but some basics (like support for reconciling cash and shares to online balances) are not there, resulting in much manual labor compared to the Quicken for Windows.  On the positive side, Quicken for Mac is reasonably responsive, while Quicken for Windows became painfully slow (running within a virtual machine on even the fastest Mac).  Intuit needs to improve this program.  The competition isn't much better but others are gradually improving their offerings.  Update: Quicken for Mac (2015 or 2016) does not work with T. Rowe Price retirement accounts, although brokerage accounts should work.  TRP offers no solutions for this.  Also, as of late 2015, importing an .OFX or .QFX file downloaded from a bank which uses this method can fail, if Quicken for Mac decides that the financial institution has not signed up with Intuit. This is beyond bad.  Intuit has no business being in the middle of bank-customer data downloads.  This raises concerns about whether Intuit is aggregating information about Quicken users' financial connections, which creates a huge security vulnerability.  For this reason, I'm downgrading Quicken for Mac to only two stars.

I was skeptical that a downloadable version of office could really be an excellent program, but I was totally wrong. This is absolutely the best version yet. The one adjustment is to go into the advanced setup and turn off graphics acceleration.If you don't, many of your games will run very slowly. Just uncheck the box and restart any of the programs: it will run even faster without the acceleration, and all your games will hum along as before.

Among the new features, two stand-out: the app store and the spell checker. The app store gives you free access to such programs as The Merriam Webster Dictionary and Legal Zoom Forms. It feels as though you own an iPhone. The add-ins work flawlessly and there are so many that it is absolutely fun to find them. The spell checker in Word solves so many problems that it is worth the money by itself. Not only does it work in the whole document instead of that maddening small window of the past, but it also has a superior ability to find whole words that have accidentally been split by commas or semi-colons. I actually saw it find "did;nt" and offer the correct replacement -- something it was never able to do in the past.

As far as the subscription "tether" - well, if $100 brings all of this, then I welcome it. Every year. Updates come in automatically and smoothly.

One caveat: if you have previously added-in classic menu toolbars in your older versions, disable them. If you haven't, Office 365 will try to use them and then be unable to do so when it starts up. it will search for a way for several minutes before any program, such as Word or Excel, starts. You must go into the setup to add-ins for EACH program and uncheck them (COM add-ins). It is a royal pain. So, disable all those classic menu add-ins before downloading.

Other than that, a superb product, well worth more than the$100 price.

If your bank isn't on the list, plan on entering each of your transactions manually. I'm sure this product is fine if your accounts are with a major banking institution.  I would be leery if you bank with a credit union or regional bank though.
